item.title: Running it: signals, restarts and what it says
item.description:
It reads everything once

The configuration files and the keytab are read at start. There is no reload of them, and the packaged unit has no ExecReload=. After changing either:

sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd
sudo systemctl restart authnd

The TLS certificate is the exception since v0.15.0: authnd looks atcert_file and key_file again, so a renewal needs no restart. Seerenewing the certificate.

Apart from the sources (below), the one thing applied while it runs is apassword a person changes through authnd,which re-reads the user blocks and nothing else.

The sources are the exception to “read once”. People and groups are read again every refresh (60 s by default; refresh = "0" turns it off) into a new snapshot built off the serving path and swapped in atomically, so a removed person or group member is gone within one period, with no restart. (v0.13.4 read them once and needed a restart for a change to a group.) A refresh that fails keeps the last good data and is logged once per failure streak, naming the source. Where revocation matters, set max_age (for example "10m"): once the data is older, searches, people’s binds and password changes answerunavailable (52) instead of stale data. A source that cannot be read at start, such as a groups query that does not run or one of several databases being down, refuses the start and check, naming the source and the group. An entry too large for one LDAP message (about 3 MiB, which one 10 MB attribute value is enough to reach) is not published, and is said at start and by check, like an entry that fails the schema.

Signals

signal what happens
SIGTERM, SIGINT it prints stopping, closes the listeners and every established connection, stops the realm, closes the sources, and exits 0 once the server has really finished
SIGHUP it is caught and logged, and authnd stays up. It reads the TLS certificate again at once (v0.15.0); the configuration and the keytab are not reloaded 
$ authnd --config etc/authnd
ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 1 person from the configuration file
hangup: authnd does not reload its configuration or keytab; restart it to apply those (the TLS certificate is read again)
alice's password change was refused: the old password did not verify: directory: wrong password
alice changed their own password
stopping

That is one run of the v0.15.0 binary: a kill -HUP, two attempts to change a password (the first refused, the second accepted), then a kill -TERM.The process was still there after the SIGHUP.

A SIGHUP used to kill authnd — Go’s default for a signal nobody handles— and systemd counts death by SIGHUP as a clean exit, soRestart=on-failure did not start it again: one kill -HUP or one logrotatepostrotate took a directory down for good. It is caught now so that the habit is harmless, and the line says what to do instead.

Closing established connections, not only the listener, is deliberate: a server that stopped accepting and left its open connections answering would look stopped and not be, which is the restart that does not take.

What it writes

Everything goes to standard output, which under systemd is the journal(journalctl -u authnd):

  • at start, where it listens and whom it serves — ldap on …, ldaps on … or ldap+starttls on …, then realm EXAMPLE.ORG on … (udp and tcp) with akerberos block;
  • every refused bind under an mfa block, every refused token, every refused or completed password change, with the reason — which the client is never told; see the second factor and tokens;
  • every request the KDC refuses, prefixed kerberos:, with the Kerberos error code; see the realm;
  • the LDAP library’s own log, in slog text form, at level info.

A plain wrong password on a simple bind, with no mfa block, is answeredinvalidCredentials and not logged by authnd itself.

Limits and deadlines

From v0.15.0 authnd bounds what a client, a slow source or a flood can make it hold. Four optional keys, at the top level of the configuration:

key default meaning
max_connections 4096 (it was unlimited) the most connections open at once; 0 is unlimited
max_connections_per_ip none the most from one address; it may not exceed max_connections
operation_timeout 30s (it was none) the longest one LDAP operation may take; "0" is none, otherwise at least 100ms
startup_timeout 60s the longest opening and first reading of every source may take; "0" is none

A connection over a cap is sent busy (51) in a notice of disconnection and closed, never queued (RFC 4511 4.4.1). An operation still running atoperation_timeout is answered timeLimitExceeded (3), even when its handler is blocked and ignores the deadline: the late result is dropped. A source that does not answer at start makes authnd refuse to start after startup_timeout,with an error that names the stage and the source. A negative number, or a duration that does not parse, is refused at start and by check. Setmax_connections = 0 and operation_timeout = "0" for v0.14’s behaviour.

check prints the limits it will serve with, so that nobody runs the defaults without knowing:

$ authnd check etc2/authnd
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
limits: 200 connections, 20 per address; an operation may take 10s; startup may take no limit
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
staff alice groupOfNames
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
a bind carries a password
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

That configuration says max_connections = 200, max_connections_per_ip = 20,operation_timeout = "10s" and startup_timeout = "0". Without those four keys the line reads limits: 4096 connections, no limit per address; an operation may take 30s; startup may take 1m0s, which the same binary printed too.

An outage is not a wrong password

When the people are checked against another directory (an ldap source) and that directory cannot be asked, because the connection is refused or reset, it answers busy, unavailable or other, or it does not answer withinoperation_timeout, authnd answers LDAP unavailable (52), never invalidCredentials (49). That holds for a simple bind, for the old password of a password change and for the password factor of an mfa bind. Before v0.15.0 it was reported as a wrong password, so a client such as a login form told the person the password was wrong while the directory was down. A wrong password is still 49. The cause is in the log, not in what the client is told, and an outage is not counted as a failed guess.

When it does not start

A refusal is one line on standard error, prefixed authnd:, and exit status 1; under the unit, Restart=on-failure then tries again every five seconds and the line is in the journal each time. Everything check refuses is refused here too, and the one thing only the server finds is an address it cannot listen on — seecheck.The LDAP listener, the certificate and the realm are all opened before the first line is printed, so a server that cannot start prints only the refusal. Here a second instance meets the first one’s Kerberos port:

$ authnd --config cases/realm2
authnd: kerberos udp 127.0.0.1:18388: listen udp 127.0.0.1:18388: bind: address already in use

The ldap on … line, and realm … on … after it, mean both halves are listening.

Telling that it is up

There is no health endpoint and no metrics. What there is:

  • the process and its exit status — under systemd, systemctl is-active authnd. If the LDAP listener or the realm stops of its own accord, the whole process ends with that error, so a live process is one whose two halves both answer;
  • the root DSE, which answers an anonymous client and says which version it is talking to:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' '+' '*'
dn:
objectClass: top
objectClass: OpenLDAProotDSE
supportedLDAPVersion: 3
namingContexts: dc=example,dc=org
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1
supportedControl: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.319
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.1
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.2
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.1
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.3
subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema
vendorName: go-authn/authnd
vendorVersion: v0.13.0

On a StartTLS listener that query needs -ZZ. A probe that proves more — that a source still answers — is a bind as a person or a reader kept for the purpose; with ausers "ldap" block, that bind reaches the directory behind this one.

What lives where, and what a restart loses

configuration, passwords, DSN, certificate, keytab the files the configuration names; nothing is copied
a SQLite database wherever its DSN says; /var/lib/authnd under the unit
second-factor counts and lockouts memory only: a restart forgets them, including a person locked out after a hundred wrong codes
used one-time codes memory only
